NEXORA — ULTRA-DEEP FORENSIC SECURITY, QUALITY, RELIABILITY AND REPAIR MISSION
MASTER EXECUTION PROMPT FOR GOOGLE AI STUDIO / GEMINI
Version: 1.0 | Prepared from the supplied NEXORA source archive

MISSION MODE: STRICT • EVIDENCE-DRIVEN • ZERO-SKIP • DEFENSIVE • REPAIR-AND-VERIFY

READ THIS ENTIRE DOCUMENT BEFORE EDITING ANY FILE.

You are acting simultaneously as a principal application-security engineer, senior
full-stack engineer, cloud/Firebase security specialist, payments-integrity engineer,
AI-security specialist, QA lead, SRE, privacy engineer, accessibility reviewer,
and pragmatic SaaS architect. You have been given the owner's NEXORA repository.
Your job is not to praise it, merely describe it, or produce another audit document.
Your job is to inspect every relevant file, independently reproduce every finding,
identify every additional defect you can discover, implement the safest maintainable
fixes, add regression tests, execute the tests, and leave the repository in a verified
working state. Treat the existing audit reports as claims to verify, never as truth.

THE NON-NEGOTIABLE NO-SKIP DIRECTIVE
1. Do not skip a finding because it is small, tedious, repetitive, low-risk, or awkward.
2. Do not stop after fixing only the Critical or High findings.
3. Do not silently omit any file, route, rule, handler, UI action, export, configuration,
   dependency, test, or generated asset that may affect security or correctness.
4. Do not mark an issue fixed until the exact source change exists and a regression test
   demonstrates that the previous failure is blocked and legitimate use still works.
5. Do not replace a real implementation with a mock, fake success, hard-coded result,
   empty catch, stub, TODO, or decorative UI.
6. Do not claim a build, test, deployment, penetration test, or live verification ran
   unless you actually executed it and captured the output in the evidence ledger.
7. If an environment, dependency, credential, emulator, tool, or permission prevents
   verification, record the exact blocker, classify the result as NOT VERIFIED, and
   provide a reproducible next command. Never convert an unverified item to PASS.
8. Do not delete functionality simply to make a test pass. Preserve intended behavior,
   data compatibility, and the product's core capabilities. Where a feature is only a
   prototype, label it honestly and prevent the UI from claiming it is operational.
9. Keep a persistent finding register. Every discovered issue gets a unique ID, exact
   path and line/function reference, severity, exploit preconditions, consequence,
   reproduction, fix, test, result, and residual-risk note.
10. Continue in batches when context or execution limits require it. Save progress in
    files inside the repository and resume from the last unfinished finding. Do not
    restart, discard, or summarize away the backlog. Do not ask the owner to repeat
    information already present in the repository or this prompt.

SECURITY BOUNDARY — AUTHORISED DEFENSIVE TESTING ONLY
This is an audit of the supplied owner's code. Perform attacker-style simulations only
against a local instance, local mock server, Firebase Emulator Suite, Netlify Dev, or
other explicitly isolated test environment with synthetic accounts and synthetic data.
Never probe, exploit, stress, fuzz, enumerate, or send crafted payloads to production,
real customers, third-party services, public infrastructure, or any domain you do not
own and control. Do not attempt real account takeover, credential theft, payment fraud,
exfiltration, destructive writes, denial-of-service, or real webhook replay. Do not use
real customer records. Do not use real payment credentials. Use provider sandbox/test
mode and synthetic test events only. Do not expose API keys, bearer tokens, private keys,
service-account credentials, customer data, or secrets in logs or reports. Never print
secret values. Use redacted fingerprints/variable names only. Never deploy automatically.
Never run destructive migrations against production. Require a human owner review for
irreversible or external side effects. Attack simulations below are test specifications,
not permission to target a live endpoint.

IMPORTANT SECURITY REALITY
No software can be promised "non-hackable". Aim for least privilege, deny-by-default,
secure defaults, strong authentication, server-authoritative authorization, isolation,
validated state transitions, supply-chain hygiene, observability, backup/recovery,
regular patching, and defence in depth. Explain residual risks honestly.

actual extracted workspace, not just this prompt. The observed repository includes:

  alongside the primary index.html SPA. Verify whether they are used before removal.

FIRST-PASS FINDINGS THAT MUST BE RE-VERIFIED AND REPAIRED
The following are reported observations from a preliminary source review. They are
not a substitute for fresh line-by-line inspection. Re-open each file, confirm whether
it remains true in the current workspace, find all related copies/callers, and either
fix it or document a justified false positive with evidence. Do not simply paste this
list into a report. Implement the repair and prove it.

F-001 | CRITICAL | AI identity/authentication bypass
File: functions/src/ai/copilotService.ts, around lines 483-502.
Reported behavior: a live request can bypass mandatory bearer-token verification when
client body supplies permissionGranted or any non-null userData. Invalid bearer token
verification is caught and ignored in one branch while client identity can remain.
Fix: require valid Firebase ID token for every non-demo live request before using body;
ignore client-supplied identity/role/org as authority; derive UID and claims server-side;
fail closed on invalid/missing/expired/revoked token; never swallow verification errors.
Regression: missing token, forged body identity, permissionGranted=true, empty object,
invalid token, expired token, revoked token, token for different project, and valid user.

F-002 | CRITICAL | Client-controlled AI consent
File: functions/src/ai/copilotService.ts around lines 513-517; index.html around 538-560.
Reported behavior: consent may be inferred from permissionGranted=true or userData != null;
localStorage is treated as a source of truth and Firestore persistence failure can still
show success. Fix: consent must be a server-verified, explicit, per-user/per-org record;
store policy version, timestamp, scope, actor, revocation and purpose. Check server-side
on every data-bearing AI call. Local state is UI-only. Deny on missing/error/revoked consent.

F-003 | CRITICAL | Client-controlled tenant context and private data
File: functions/src/ai/copilotService.ts around lines 530-610; index.html around 761-892.
Reported behavior: userData/orgId/history/userRole/userName can be passed by browser as
AI context. Fix: accept only narrow validated query/intent from browser; fetch authorized
records server-side using verified UID + active membership + scoped orgId; enforce field
allowlist, data minimisation, redaction and per-request caps. Do not ship full tenant
snapshots to an external model by default. Provide explicit preview of records sent.

F-004 | CRITICAL | Demo fixtures contaminate live AI context
File: functions/src/ai/copilotService.ts around lines 531-610.
Reported behavior: empty userData arrays can be filled with synthetic sample projects,
tasks or requests even when the session is not in demo mode. Fix: hard separate demo
fixtures behind verified server-side demo claims/environment. Live empty dataset means
empty dataset; never invent business records, IDs, financials or evidence.

F-005 | CRITICAL | AI role defaults to OWNER
File: functions/src/ai/copilotService.ts around lines 489-502.
Reported behavior: role fallback defaults to OWNER. Fix: role is derived from server-side
membership only; missing/unknown/inactive membership means deny; never default privilege.

F-006 | HIGH | AI prompt injection from business records/history
File: functions/src/ai/copilotService.ts, prompt assembly and history handling.
Reported risk: stored task/vendor/project/customer text can contain hostile instructions.
Fix: treat every record, attachment, note, user message, retrieved result and model output
as untrusted data; delimiter/label it; never let it override system policy or authorize
calls; constrain model to structured proposals; require deterministic server validation.

F-007 | HIGH | AI proposal validation is not a complete schema allowlist
File: functions/src/ai/copilotService.ts around lines 727-773.
Reported risk: blocked-field blacklist can miss unknown, nested, reserved or dangerous
fields and values. Fix: strict per-collection JSON schemas with additionalProperties=false,
known field allowlists, enum validation, ownership checks, type/length/range checks,
state-transition checks, server-generated timestamps and actor fields. Reject unknowns.

F-008 | HIGH | AI fallback can invent approval decisions/resource IDs
File: functions/src/ai/copilotService.ts around lines 774-799.
Reported risk: fallback inference may produce approve/reject proposals with generic IDs
such as req-501. Fix: never infer an irreversible action from natural language without
an exact authorized record selected by user; verify record exists and belongs to org;
require explicit confirmation and second authorization check at execution time.

F-009 | HIGH | AI rate limit is process-local
File: functions/src/ai/copilotService.ts around lines 156-182.
Reported risk: Map-based counter resets across serverless instances and can be bypassed
by scaling/cold starts; client identity can be spoofed; memory may grow. Fix: shared atomic
rate limiter keyed by verified UID + org + endpoint, IP abuse layer, concurrency limits,
cost/token budgets, per-plan policy and bounded cleanup. Avoid logging raw IP/PII.

F-010 | HIGH | Configurable OpenRouter URL can leak provider key / SSRF
File: functions/src/ai/copilotService.ts around lines 184-209.
Reported risk: arbitrary custom environment host is accepted with warning. Fix: strict
HTTPS origin allowlist for expected provider endpoint; reject credentials, query, fragment,
non-default ports and IP literals; do not follow unsafe redirects; never forward provider
secret to untrusted host; test malformed and alternate URL encodings.

F-011 | HIGH | AI request/response resource-exhaustion exposure
File: functions/src/ai/copilotService.ts around lines 234-314 and request parsing.
Reported risk: large prompts/history/records/output, excessive concurrent calls, long
provider wait and unbounded model costs. Fix: bounded body, messages, record count, chars,
output tokens, timeout/abort, concurrency, retries with jitter, cost ceilings and per-user
budget. Return generic errors; redact upstream diagnostics.

F-012 | MEDIUM | AI model-selection/cost policy unsafe defaults
File: functions/src/ai/copilotService.ts configuration around AI_ALLOW_PAID_MODELS.
Reported risk: paid models allowed by default or weakly restricted. Fix: explicit server
allowlist, environment-specific cost cap, allowed model IDs, no user-controlled model,
provider fallback policy, telemetry for token/cost and fail closed if policy unavailable.

F-013 | MEDIUM | AI history role/shape injection
File: functions/src/ai/copilotService.ts message history parsing.
Reported risk: caller can assign system/developer/assistant roles or inject oversized,
malformed history. Fix: accept only user turns from client or server-signed conversation
state; rebuild system prompt server-side; schema validate and cap turn count/age/bytes.

F-014 | MEDIUM | AI synthetic metrics and fake company context
File: functions/src/ai/copilotService.ts around lines 549+ and prompt/fixture definitions.
Reported risk: invented $340k, Acme Global, 15% receivable, fabricated sample records,
USD symbols despite INR settings. Fix: remove live-mode fake data; clearly badge demo data;
attach provenance/calculation details; use org currency and locale; label estimates.

F-015 | MEDIUM | AI truthiness defaults can erase valid zero values
File: AI context/calculation helpers and associated UI.
Reported risk: `value || fallback` treats legitimate 0 as missing. Fix: nullish checks,
explicit finite numeric schema and tests for 0, -0 where relevant, null and undefined.

F-016 | CRITICAL | Arbitrary API base URL can receive Firebase bearer token
File: index.html around lines 7834-7854; token-authenticated calls elsewhere.
Reported behavior: localStorage `nexora_api_base_url` is used as API base, arbitrary URL
may be accepted, and some calls send Firebase ID token to it. Fix: remove user-settable
arbitrary host in production; restrict to same-origin relative `/api` or exact validated
trusted origins; validate scheme/host/port/path before acquiring token; never attach a
bearer token to an untrusted destination. Add redirect and DNS-rebinding considerations.

F-017 | HIGH | XSS: dynamic values interpolated into HTML templates
File: index.html around renderAiCopilotDrawer (~1028), renderCopilotMessage (~1163),
testDodoConnection (~7933-7939), proposal IDs around 1229-1232, and openModal callers.
Reported examples: activeUserName/activeUserRole, msg.dataAccessStatus, p.id and provider
response fields enter innerHTML or inline onclick contexts. Fix: use DOM APIs/textContent;
context-aware escaping only as secondary defence; never use HTML escaping as JS-string
escaping; remove inline handlers; use addEventListener and opaque IDs; allowlist any markup.
Audit every `.innerHTML`, `insertAdjacentHTML`, `outerHTML`, `document.write`, URL sink,
attribute sink, CSS sink, eval/new Function and inline event handler in every file.

F-018 | HIGH | Unsafe generic openModal HTML sink
File: index.html openModal(htmlContent) and all callers.
Reported risk: raw interpolated HTML passed to modal. Fix: replace with safe template
renderer or DOM node APIs; classify each caller input as static/trusted/user/provider/model;
sanitize rich text with maintained allowlist parser; test each dynamic sink individually.

F-019 | MEDIUM | AI chat persistence on shared devices
File: index.html AI chat localStorage handling.
Reported risk: retained sensitive prompt/response after sign-out/account switch and no
retention policy. Fix: clear user-scoped caches on sign-out and account change; define TTL,
size limits, user-visible delete/export and consent; avoid storing sensitive business data.

F-020 | HIGH | False success for Firestore write in offline/missing preconditions
File: index.html around saveToFirestore 1410-1424 and updateInFirestore 1427-1453.
Reported behavior: returns success-shaped result when offline/demo/preconditions absent;
callers may show success although nothing was persisted. Fix: discriminated result types
(PERSISTED, QUEUED, DEMO_ONLY, FAILED); never report persisted unless server confirms;
make offline queue explicit and durable with conflict handling.

F-021 | HIGH | Read-then-upsert race and stale overwrites
File: index.html updateInFirestore around 1427-1453.
Reported behavior: missing doc may be upserted from local state after read. Fix: use
transaction or update-only semantics with expected version; separate create/update APIs;
conflict detection, idempotency and audit history.

F-022 | MEDIUM | Client activity log is not durable audit trail
File: index.html recordActivity around 1455-1468.
Reported risk: local-only activity list and IDs derived from last digits of Date.now collide.
Fix: server-generated immutable append-only audit events with unique IDs; trustworthy
actor/tenant/time; redact secrets; distinguish telemetry from compliance audit.

F-023 | MEDIUM | False sync-complete status
File: index.html refreshLiveData around 1471-1478.
Reported behavior: complete toast even after partial failures or early return. Fix: return
structured per-collection results; show partial/failed states; only show complete on full
success; expose sync timestamp and retry.

F-024 | CRITICAL | Live org provisioning defaults to OWNER/sample data
File: index.html syncLiveOrg around 1480 onward, especially around 1589-1593.
Reported behavior: client may set currentRole OWNER, synthetic owner membership, or seed
sample project/task into live org. Fix: server-side first-user provisioning with atomic

F-025 | HIGH | Firestore read errors treated as absent/new org
File: index.html syncLiveOrg and Firestore collection loading.
Reported behavior: permission/network errors may be treated like missing documents and

F-026 | HIGH | Firestore reads silently fall back to empty docs
File: index.html syncLiveOrg collection reads.
Reported risk: read failure presented as empty business. Fix: surface per-collection error,

F-027 | MEDIUM | Multiple organization memberships not modelled safely
File: index.html syncLiveOrg / currentOrg selection.
Reported behavior: derives a deterministic org ID from UID and may ignore membership list.

F-028 | MEDIUM | Hard-coded New York timezone and USD defaults

F-029 | HIGH | No pagination/limits on client Firestore reads

F-030 | HIGH | Org settings can show success after failed write

END OF FIRST-PASS FINDING REGISTER. FIND MORE. This register is a floor, not a ceiling.

PHASE 0 — WORKSPACE SAFETY AND BASELINE
A. Confirm the repository root and enumerate all files, including hidden files and nested
   source, tests, scripts, configs, docs, static assets, generated bundles and lockfiles.
B. Record hashes, sizes, file types, symlinks and executable bits. Do not read external
   files outside the provided workspace unless they are standard package documentation.
C. Make a reversible Git checkpoint/branch or copy before edits. Do not overwrite user work.
D. Inspect `.gitignore`, `.env.example`, tracked files and repository history for secrets.
   Never print candidate values; report path, type, and redacted fingerprint only.
E. Identify actual app entry point and deployment target(s). Reconstruct build graph and
   dependency graph. Do not assume a script is used merely because it exists.
F. Capture baseline package install/build/typecheck/test output if possible. Record exact
   commands, versions, exit codes and logs. If dependencies cannot install, continue static
   analysis and state precisely what was blocked.
G. Never run deploy, migration, payment, real email, external webhook, load test or deletion.
H. Add `AUDIT/MASTER_FINDING_REGISTER.md`, `AUDIT/ATTACK_TEST_MATRIX.md`,
   `AUDIT/REPAIR_LEDGER.md`, `AUDIT/VERIFICATION_EVIDENCE.md`, and `AUDIT/RESIDUAL_RISK.md`.
I. Save intermediate progress after each phase. Each finding ID in this prompt must get a
   terminal status: FIXED+VERIFIED, FIXED+NOT_VERIFIED, NOT_REPRODUCED+EVIDENCE,
   ACCEPTED_RISK+OWNER_REASON, or BLOCKED+EXACT_REASON. No blank statuses.

PHASE 1 — REPOSITORY-WIDE FORENSIC INSPECTION
Inspect every file in the repository. Do not rely on grep alone. Read whole relevant files,
understand call graph and data flows, and inspect every caller/callee of each risky helper.
Search for and review all occurrences of:
- `innerHTML`, `outerHTML`, `insertAdjacentHTML`, `document.write`, `srcdoc`.
- `onclick=`, `onerror=`, `onload=`, other inline event handlers and string callbacks.
- `eval`, `Function`, dynamic import, dynamic script loading, unsafe URL construction.
- `fetch`, Axios, XMLHttpRequest, WebSocket, EventSource, redirects and postMessage.
- Authorization, Bearer, ID token, refresh token, cookies, localStorage and sessionStorage.
- Firestore reads/writes, collectionGroup, transactions, batch writes and security rules.
- Admin role, platform owner, orgId, userId, membership, invite, approval, status changes.
- Dodo APIs, checkout, customer portal, webhook signature, subscription and plan mapping.
- AI prompts, retrieved context, model output, tool/action proposals, provider URL and keys.
- `catch`, empty catch, fallback, `||`, `??`, default, hard-coded sample data and success toast.
- `TODO`, `FIXME`, `HACK`, `mock`, `demo`, `fake`, `sample`, `placeholder`, `stub`.
- CSV/JSON exports, file uploads/downloads, import parsing, URL previews and QR scanning.
- Logging, telemetry, error handlers, diagnostics, stack traces, debug endpoints.
- Pagination, sorting, query filters, limits, retries, timeouts, concurrency and rate limits.
- Date arithmetic, currencies, decimal/floating arithmetic and financial rounding.
For each pattern, distinguish safe uses from unsafe contexts. Build a sink/source map.
Trace untrusted data from source to sink and authorization decision; don't simply replace
all occurrences mechanically.

PHASE 2 — THREAT MODEL
Define assets: tenant documents, member profiles, credentials, sessions, customer details,
financial records, invoices, billing/subscription state, payment provider metadata, AI prompts,
model outputs, audit history, exports, platform-admin actions, API keys and availability.
Define trust boundaries: browser, local storage, frontend bundle, API adapter, Firebase Auth,
Firestore Rules, Admin SDK, server runtime, Netlify/Firebase hosting, Dodo, OpenRouter,
email service, background worker, browser extensions and user-supplied imports.
Define actors: anonymous visitor, authenticated non-member, invited member, suspended member,
former member, viewer, employee, manager, org admin, org owner, platform admin, malicious
insider, compromised user account, hostile tenant, malicious vendor text, prompt-injection
content, webhook attacker and accidental operator.
Define security objectives: confidentiality, integrity, availability, tenant isolation,
least privilege, non-repudiation, financial correctness, privacy, consent, recovery, auditability.
Use STRIDE or equivalent to model spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure,
denial of service and elevation of privilege for every trust boundary and critical flow.
Write a data classification and retention policy. Treat PII, business financial data and
provider secrets as sensitive; define what the AI provider may receive and on what consent.

PHASE 3 — SEVERITY AND PRIORITISATION
Use a consistent risk rubric. CRITICAL: unauthenticated or low-privilege remote compromise,
admin/owner escalation, cross-tenant private data exposure, payment/subscription fraud,
secret compromise, arbitrary privileged writes, widespread data destruction, or systemic
authorization bypass. HIGH: substantial account/tenant compromise, material data exposure,
financial manipulation, reliable stored/reflected XSS, serious workflow abuse. MEDIUM:
limited exploitability or meaningful integrity/privacy/availability issue with prerequisites.
LOW: minor weakness, robustness, consistency, usability or maintainability with limited
security effect. INFO: no defect but hardening recommendation. Include likelihood, impact,
exploit complexity, privileges, scope, detectability and business impact. Use CVSS only as
an aid, not a substitute for product context. Do not inflate severity for drama.

PHASE 4 — AUTHENTICATION AND SESSION SECURITY
Verify every protected API route rejects missing, malformed, invalid, expired, revoked,
wrong-project, wrong-issuer, wrong-audience and disabled-user tokens. Check token claim
validation; do not trust decoded-but-unverified JWT fields. Verify clock skew handling.
Confirm account status and membership status at authorization time, not only login time.
Define revocation/logout behavior, cache invalidation, token renewal and session expiration.
Ensure sensitive owner/billing operations require MFA or step-up reauthentication where
supported. Verify no browser localStorage value can create authenticated identity or role.
Check sign-in, sign-out, guest, demo, invite, password reset, email verification and account
switch flows. Rate-limit auth-sensitive endpoints and prevent user enumeration. Avoid raw
Firebase errors and stack traces. Ensure auth failures are consistent and don't leak whether
an email, UID, organization or subscription exists.

PHASE 5 — MULTI-TENANT AUTHORIZATION AND FIRESTORE
Create a canonical role/permission matrix. At minimum evaluate roles: ANONYMOUS,
AUTHENTICATED_NONMEMBER, INVITED, SUSPENDED, INACTIVE, VIEWER, EMPLOYEE, MANAGER,
ORG_ADMIN, OWNER, PLATFORM_ADMIN, SYSTEM_WORKER. Evaluate membership states:
MISSING, PENDING, ACTIVE, SUSPENDED, REVOKED, EXPIRED. Define exact expected behavior
for each resource and operation before writing tests. The default is deny.
Resources must include organizations, members, invitations, projects, project activities,
tasks, workflows, workflow runs, requests, approvals, goals, incidents, customers, vendors,
assets, knowledge articles, meetings, dashboards, reports, AI proposals, AI consent, AI audit,
notifications, usage, billing, webhook events, admin audit, owner configuration, support notes.
Operations must include get, list, create, update, delete, query, export, batch, transaction,
collectionGroup, and subcollection access. Inspect document fields and query constraints.
Ensure tenantId/orgId cannot be changed by a normal member. Ensure every query is scoped to
active organization and Firestore rules can prove query constraints. Do not rely on client
filtering. Validate ownership at server endpoints too. Do not assume Admin SDK obeys rules.
Any server-side Admin SDK access must perform equivalent authorization explicitly.
Rules should use helper functions consistently and avoid duplicated logic. Check rules
language syntax, function argument limits, call depth, get/exists access budgets and query
limits. Emulator tests must use actual Firestore rules and synthetic users, not mocked
helper functions. Ensure production rules are canonical and no duplicate stale rules file
is accidentally deployed or displayed as current.

PHASE 6 — CROSS-TENANT ATTACK SIMULATION
Create at least Tenant-A and Tenant-B with distinct records and users. Use IDs that look
valid but are deliberately guessed, copied, substituted, encoded, malformed and stale.
Attempt access to Tenant-B by Tenant-A member through every route, direct Firestore path,
collection query, document reference, export, search, notification, billing operation,
AI context, workflow trigger, owner action and import. Every attempt must be denied without
revealing the existence or contents of another tenant's records. Test org switch, multiple
memberships, revoked user, deleted org, orphan membership and owner transfer. Never use
real accounts or data. Store test results with redacted synthetic IDs only.

PHASE 7 — INPUT VALIDATION, BUSINESS LOGIC AND STATE MACHINES
Define strict DTO schemas for every endpoint. Reject unknown keys, wrong types, invalid
IDs, oversized strings, deeply nested values, arrays above caps, unexpected content types,
malformed JSON, duplicate keys where parser supports detection, numeric overflow, NaN,
Infinity, unsafe integers, invalid dates and unsupported enums. Normalize safely without
changing meaning. Use server-generated actor/time/org fields. Prevent mass assignment.
Define explicit state machines for requests, approvals, tasks, incidents, workflows, invites,
subscriptions, checkouts, webhook events and owner incidents. Enforce transition matrix on
server in atomic transaction; UI state is never authority. Add optimistic concurrency/version
checks and idempotency for retried operations.

PHASE 8 — PAYMENT AND WEBHOOK SECURITY
Use official Dodo SDK documentation/current version and sandbox mode. Verify exact signature
algorithm, header names, timestamp tolerance, raw body bytes and constant-time comparison.
Never accept `unsafeUnwrap` for production. Reject missing or malformed signature. Ensure
webhook endpoint is isolated from normal JSON parser so signature bytes are preserved.
Implement atomic event claim/deduplication and idempotent side effects. Reconcile events by
provider customer/subscription IDs against immutable server mappings. Validate product ID,
plan, amount, currency, event type, status, provider timestamp and organization. Prevent
stale/reordered events from downgrading or reactivating wrong subscriptions. Use outbox/saga
for multi-document operations; a failed write must not be marked processed. Add retry/lease
and dead-letter operations. Ensure owner retry endpoint is idempotent and tightly authorized.
Never test using a real payment or real customer. Never disclose secret values.

PHASE 9 — AI SECURITY AND DATA GOVERNANCE
Treat the browser, user text, stored records, uploaded files, retrieved documents, model
response and provider metadata as untrusted. Verify caller identity and active membership
first. Obtain server-verified consent for the exact scope and purpose. Minimize and redact
context. Protect against direct and indirect prompt injection, tool/role confusion, data
exfiltration requests, secret extraction, cross-tenant retrieval, hallucinated citations,
false numerical claims, fabricated records, unauthorized actions, model denial-of-service,
provider abuse, model-cost blowout, provider outage and poisoned history.
Do not give model output authority. Model may propose a typed action only; deterministic
server code validates schema, target, tenant, role, resource version, limits and policy.
High-impact action requires exact record, explicit user confirmation, and fresh server-side
authorization before commit. Keep a full provenance trail. Do not expose system prompts or
secrets. Ensure configured provider URL is strict allowlist and redirects cannot leak keys.

PHASE 10 — FRONTEND AND BROWSER SECURITY
Audit every HTML/DOM sink with its exact rendering context. Prefer textContent and DOM APIs.
Do not concatenate untrusted input into HTML, JS, CSS, URL, event handlers or attributes.
Remove inline event handlers and adopt safe event delegation. Use CSP with nonce/hash or
bundled scripts; avoid unsafe-inline/eval unless a documented exception is essential.
Pin dependencies and verify SRI when loading third-party assets. Protect against clickjacking,
open redirects, DOM clobbering, prototype pollution, unsafe URL schemes, tabnabbing, CSRF
where cookie auth is used, postMessage origin confusion, service-worker cache poisoning,
localStorage token leakage and browser extension assumptions. Ensure client configuration
cannot exfiltrate bearer tokens. Test logout, shared device, browser back button, stale cache,
multiple tabs, offline mode and account switching.

PHASE 11 — PRIVACY AND DATA LIFECYCLE
Inventory personal/business data collected, stored, derived, transmitted and logged. Define
purpose, legal basis/consent where applicable, data minimization, access, correction, export,
retention, deletion, backup retention, subprocessors, data residency and breach response.
Avoid sending customer/financial/personally identifying data to AI provider unless explicitly
necessary, consented and covered by the product's privacy terms. Redact logs, traces, support
exports and analytics. Ensure account deletion and org deletion are complete, transactional
or resumable, and protect legal/financial record retention requirements. Do not invent legal
compliance claims; flag jurisdiction-specific legal review to owner.

PHASE 12 — RELIABILITY, PERFORMANCE AND OPERATIONS
Check timeouts, retries, retry storms, circuit breakers, memory growth, unbounded arrays,
query scan cost, serverless cold starts, concurrency, rate limits, queue backlog, pagination,
indexes, caching, stale cache invalidation, storage quota, file limits, graceful shutdown,
health/readiness separation, alerting, secrets rotation, backup restore, disaster recovery,
RTO/RPO, deployment rollback, monitoring and error budgets. No fake performance metrics.
Test large-but-safe synthetic datasets locally, with capped load and no external traffic.

PHASE 13 — FINANCIAL AND NUMERICAL CORRECTNESS
Use integer minor units for monetary storage and arithmetic where possible. Keep currency
with every amount. Never add unlike currencies without an explicit conversion rate/source/
time. Validate safe integers and rounding rules. Test monthly/annual billing prorations,
zero amount, negative refund, tax, discount, credit, failed/reversed payment, partial payment,
overpayment, cancelled/expired subscriptions, leap years, month-end boundaries, time zones,
DST and duplicate transactions. Distinguish MRR, ARR, cash collected, revenue recognized,
receivables, payables, net burn, gross margin and runway. Show insufficient data distinctly.
Never fabricate financial metrics or use USD in INR organizations.

PHASE 14 — TESTING REQUIREMENTS
Build real unit, integration, emulator, contract, regression, UI and security tests. Tests must
run against actual modules and policies, not merely test that a function returns a constant.
For each vulnerability create: precondition, synthetic fixture, exact request/operation,
expected status/result, expected no-side-effect assertion, and valid-control test. Verify
both denial and normal allowed use. Include negative, positive, boundary, concurrency and
retry cases. Avoid writing tests that assert only a status code when state may still mutate.
Inspect the database after every attack case to ensure no unauthorized change occurred.
Use local emulators, local function host, Netlify Dev and Dodo sandbox only. Never run tests
against production. Report exact test command, case count, pass/fail/skip and environment.

PHASE 15 — BUILD, STATIC ANALYSIS AND DEPENDENCY HYGIENE
Perform clean install from lockfile, lint/typecheck, unit tests, emulator rules tests, build,
production bundle inspection and smoke test. Pin versions and resolve vulnerable dependencies
with compatible upgrades; review changelogs and breaking changes. Avoid indiscriminate `npm
update`. Run static analysis for secrets, SAST, dependency audit, license inventory and
bundle inspection. Ensure source maps do not expose secrets. Check tree-shaking and public
asset copies. Keep Node and TypeScript versions compatible across root/functions/Netlify.

PHASE 16 — FIX ORDER AND CHANGE MANAGEMENT
Fix Critical issues first, then High, Medium, Low. However, work through every item. Group
changes by coherent security boundary. After each group run targeted tests; after all groups
run full suite. Preserve backwards compatibility where safe; create explicit migration plans
for schema/rules changes. Add migration scripts only when needed and make them idempotent,
reversible where possible, and separately approved. Do not run production migrations.
Keep diffs focused. Do not make a massive blind rewrite. Update docs, setup and operator runbook.

PHASE 17 — FINAL ACCEPTANCE GATES
Do not call the task complete until all of these are true or explicitly documented BLOCKED:
1. Every file has been inventoried and classified.
2. Every F-001 through F-130 has a status and evidence.
3. Every discovered additional finding has a unique ID and evidence.
4. Every sensitive route has route/method/auth/tenant/role tests.
5. Every Firestore collection and nested path has rules tests for all roles/statuses.
6. Cross-tenant attacks fail with no state change.
7. No client-trusted identity, org, role, consent or billing plan remains authoritative.
8. AI uses server-owned context and structured validation; live data never becomes fake demo data.
9. Webhook signature, atomic idempotency, retry/reconciliation and provider ownership pass.
10. DOM sinks, URL sinks and external scripts are audited and covered.
11. Entitlement limits are atomically enforced on every write path.
12. Finance results are correct for boundaries and documented policies.
13. No fake success, fake counts, fake health, fake performance or false audit claim remains.
14. Deployment adapters are canonical or parity-tested and truly deployable.
15. Internal prompts/secrets are not copied into public build output.
16. All test evidence is generated from actual execution, not manually typed totals.
17. Docs accurately distinguish implemented, prototype, disabled and future features.
18. A clean build/test run is recorded or blockers are explicit.
19. Residual risks and owner actions are listed, with severity and rationale.
20. No production deployment or external side effect occurred.

OUTPUT FORMAT INSIDE THE REPOSITORY
Create and maintain these deliverables:
- AUDIT/MASTER_FINDING_REGISTER.md — all findings, unique IDs, exact evidence/lines.
- AUDIT/ATTACK_TEST_MATRIX.md — local-only scenarios, inputs, expected and observed.
- AUDIT/REPAIR_LEDGER.md — file, diff summary, reason, migration, tests and status.
- AUDIT/VERIFICATION_EVIDENCE.md — exact executed commands, versions and results.
- AUDIT/RESIDUAL_RISK.md — unresolved, blocked, accepted, limitations and owner actions.
- Updated README.md — truthful architecture, setup, environment and feature maturity.
Add actual automated tests under the current test framework or a justified test framework.
Avoid dumping secrets or real customer identifiers into any document.

HOW TO RESPOND WHILE EXECUTING
Do not send an early celebratory summary. Work directly on the repository. When context
limits are near, save state and clearly identify the next finding IDs and next test batch.
If you cannot continue modifying files, provide a precise checkpoint, not a false claim.
Do not promise that the model will work for 40 minutes or one hour; instead maximize the
work actually executed in this session and report exact scope. Do not wait artificially.

BEGIN NOW. First inventory and read the full repository. Then independently reproduce
F-001 through F-130 and proceed through the exhaustive matrices that follow. Do not skip.

CONCRETE ATTACKER-SIMULATION PLAYBOOK — LOCAL / EMULATOR ONLY
Before any HTTP example: set LOCAL_API_BASE only to a loopback local service you own (127.0.0.1 or localhost). Abort if hostname is not loopback. Use only synthetic IDs and emulator data. Never place a real ID token or API secret in these examples.
Use fake token strings such as SYNTHETIC_INVALID_TOKEN. Use emulator-issued synthetic users only when a valid token is needed. The purpose is to prove denial and absence of side effects.

A. AI COPILOT AUTH BYPASS TEST
POST $LOCAL_API_BASE/api/ai/copilot
Content-Type: application/json
Body: {"message":"Summarize the organization","permissionGranted":true,"userId":"victim-user","userRole":"OWNER","orgId":"tenant-B","userData":{}}
Expected: 401 without valid bearer token. Body claims must not authenticate, grant consent, assign role, or select a tenant. Confirm no provider call and no database read/write.
Repeat with `userData: {projects:[],tasks:[],requests:[]}` and with `permissionGranted:false`; both still require auth. Empty object must not be interpreted as consent.
Repeat with `Authorization: Bearer SYNTHETIC_INVALID_TOKEN` plus OWNER body fields. Expected: 401; do not swallow verification failure.
Repeat with a valid synthetic Tenant-A user and body `orgId:"tenant-B"`; expected: deny or ignore body orgId and stay in Tenant-A only.

B. ROLE / IDENTITY / MEMBERSHIP SPOOFING
Submit synthetic JSON variants: {"userRole":"OWNER"}, {"role":"PLATFORM_ADMIN"}, {"isAdmin":true}, {"owner":true}, {"uid":"another-user"}, {"orgId":"other-tenant"}.
Expected: server uses verified token UID plus active membership document and server-side claims only. Unknown, missing, revoked, suspended, expired or pending membership is denied.
Call every owner route as viewer, employee, manager, org admin and ordinary owner. Only explicit policy may allow it; platform-owner-only routes must reject all non-platform identities.

C. FIRESTORE RULES PRIVILEGE ESCALATION
In Emulator Suite, as org admin attempt member create with role OWNER and status ACTIVE. Expected: deny unless secure owner-provisioning pathway explicitly authorizes it.
As a member update another member role to PLATFORM_ADMIN, OWNER, ORG_ADMIN, or change UID/orgId/status. Expected: deny.
As a suspended/revoked/pending member read each tenant path. Expected: deny even if the membership document exists.
As requester update own submitted request fields `{status:"APPROVED", approverUid:"self", decidedAt:"..."}`. Expected: deny and preserve original record.
As ordinary member alter workflow run state to COMPLETED, change owner, or inject privileged action metadata. Expected: deny or server-only transition.
As client create an audit record with forged actor, event outcome, IP or admin action. Expected: deny; trusted server writes immutable audit.

D. CROSS-TENANT IDOR / BOLA
Create two synthetic orgs A and B. Sign in as active member of A. Replace every resource ID with a known synthetic B ID for GET, LIST, UPDATE, DELETE, EXPORT, SEARCH, and AI context.
Expected: no access to B, no indication whether B record exists beyond the documented response policy, and no mutation in B. Repeat with guessed, encoded, stale, orphaned and deleted-org IDs.
Repeat using query params, path params, JSON bodies, nested resource references, collectionGroup queries, export filters, pagination cursors and workflow action payloads.

E. XSS / DOM-CONTEXT TEST VECTORS
Only insert into local synthetic test records. Use harmless markers; do not contact external URLs or execute destructive code.
HTML text marker: `<img src=x onerror=alert(1)>` — expected to display as text or be safely sanitized; no event executes.
SVG marker: `<svg onload=alert(1)>` — expected inert; no event executes.
Attribute marker: `" autofocus onfocus=alert(1) x="` — expected attribute-safe and inert.
JavaScript string marker: `');alert(1);//` — expected never to enter inline JavaScript because inline handlers are removed.
URL marker: `javascript:alert(1)` — expected rejected by URL allowlist; never assigned to href/src.
Markdown marker: `[open](javascript:alert(1))` — expected rendered as inert text or safe link; no dangerous scheme.
Test each source separately: user name, role, project/task title, notification body, AI response, proposal ID, provider diagnostic field, URL query, localStorage, Firestore document, CSV import and error message.

F. API BASE URL / BEARER TOKEN EXFILTRATION TEST
Set localStorage `nexora_api_base_url` to `https://example.invalid/collect` in a test browser with request interception. Trigger every authenticated API action.
Expected: app rejects configuration or uses only same-origin `/api`; no Authorization header is ever sent to example.invalid. No request is actually sent to the external domain; intercept and abort.
Also test `//example.invalid`, `https://user:pass@example.invalid`, `javascript:...`, `data:...`, URL-encoded host tricks, trailing-dot hosts and alternate ports; all rejected.

G. OPEN REDIRECT TESTS
In local checkout and customer-portal calls, submit returnUrl values `https://example.invalid/`, `//example.invalid`, `\example.invalid`, `javascript:alert(1)`, `data:text/html,...`, userinfo URLs and encoded variants.
Expected: 400 validation error or safe canonical app URL; never redirect or create a provider session using an untrusted return destination.

H. WEBHOOK SIGNATURE / REPLAY / EVENT ORDER TESTS
Use Dodo sandbox fixtures and local webhook handler only. Send missing signature, fake signature, tampered raw body, malformed JSON, stale timestamp, duplicate event ID and mismatched customer/product/currency.
Expected: invalid events rejected with no billing-state mutation. A valid synthetic event delivered twice concurrently produces one side effect. A failed database write remains retryable and is not marked completed.
Deliver synthetic `subscription.cancelled` then an older `subscription.active` event. Expected: older event cannot reactivate the subscription. Try unknown product ID; expected quarantine/rejection, never fallback to STARTER.

I. ENTITLEMENT AND QUOTA ABUSE
Call check-entitlement with a valid user token but another synthetic orgId. Expected: 403/404 and no organization details.
Attempt deltas 0, -1, NaN, Infinity, 1.5, unsafe integer, huge positive integer and numeric strings. Expected: only documented finite integer values accepted; unknown quota state fails closed.
Run concurrent synthetic create operations at quota boundary. Expected: atomic transaction prevents exceeding cap. Retries with same idempotency key do not double-consume quota.

J. REQUEST / APPROVAL / WORKFLOW STATE ABUSE
Try skipping directly DRAFT->APPROVED, SUBMITTED->DRAFT, CANCELLED->ACTIVE, or RESOLVED->APPROVED. Try self-approval, approver replacement, amount changes after submission, replay and stale version.
Expected: only documented transitions by authorized actors; separation of duties; every rejection leaves record and audit unchanged except a safe security event.

K. FINANCE / CSV / EXPORT ABUSE
Use synthetic amounts 0, -1, fractional minor units, NaN, Infinity, values above Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER, invalid date, unknown currency, mixed INR/USD, duplicate transaction IDs and invalid annual/monthly intervals.
Expected: documented validation or safe integer arithmetic; no silent coercion, no cross-currency sum, no false runway or fabricated 100% health.
CSV cell test values: `=1+1`, `+SUM(A1:A2)`, `-1+1`, `@SUM(1,1)`, leading TAB, CR, LF and Unicode lookalikes. Export must neutralize formula execution while preserving safely escaped data.

L. FALSE SUCCESS / PARTIAL FAILURE TESTS
Force Firestore write rejection, permission denied, network timeout, provider timeout, partial collection read and offline mode in local tests.
Expected: UI says not saved / partially synced / retry needed, never “committed” or “cloud sync complete” unless server confirms. Keep unsaved edits and show per-resource state.
Force audit persistence failure during privileged action. Expected: follow documented policy (deny critical action or durable fallback); never fabricate an audit ID and silently continue.

M. INPUT AND RESOURCE-EXHAUSTION TESTS
In local process only, submit oversized body, excessive history, deeply nested JSON, huge arrays, long strings, invalid UTF-8, malformed content-type, repeated query params and pagination abuse.
Expected: bounded 400/413/429/503 response, bounded memory/cost, abortable provider calls, no process crash, no silent parse-to-empty fallback.
Do not conduct high-volume load tests. Use small deterministic boundary fixtures and mocked clocks/providers.

N. OWNER EXPORT / DIAGNOSTICS / LOGGING TESTS
Attempt owner CSV/JSON export with ordinary member, viewer, inactive owner and valid synthetic platform admin. Enforce strict role and step-up policy.
Verify CSV formula neutralization; JSON export allowlist; diagnostics do not reveal raw errors, credentials, project topology or other tenants. Logs redact bearer tokens, API keys, webhook secrets, emails and customer fields.

O. SESSION / CACHE / SHARED DEVICE TESTS
Log in as synthetic Tenant-A user, populate AI history and data cache, log out, log in as Tenant-B user in same browser and another tab.
Expected: no A history, data, org ID, notifications, permissions or cached responses visible to B. Expire token while request is in flight; response must not persist to stale account state.
